rv.q: And yet the show, a Christmas bagatelle that is neither cynical nor syrupy, left me cheerful.
It’s a Wonderful Life: A Live Radio Play offers the modest pleasure of encountering an old acquaintance.
I think that's a big-time shame: Way more holiday fun could be had here.

Without disrespect to the artists involved — the holidays are coming, man, everybody needs a gig — this It’s a Wonderful Life isn’t so much theater as it is activity or commodity, which, it will shock nobody to hear, is always a chunk of what Broadway is.
Whatever you may think of the title, be assured it’s a wonderful show and a wonderful cast.
The cast does a terrific job all around, and creds to the very busy Foley artist Leslie Bloome, typecast as the on-stage sound effects guy.
This faithful translation of a sentimental favorite through an old-time broadcast packs a creamy double scoop of all-American nostalgia.
It’s a Wonderful Life: A Live Radio Play is still the best Christmas show on Broadway, a joyously inventive spin on a surprisingly timely story.
If the actors are so genuinely having a rousing show of it—Rannells, Hilty, Burgess, Hamlin, Rinna—it’s pretty much a cinch that the audience members will as well.
What makes the story work is the hard truths and essential lessons that enable us to overlook the dips into sentimentality.
The play is a stocking stuffer-sized treat: polished and warmly nostalgic, but also slight.
Some odd choices hinder an otherwise pleasant production.
That vintage charm wears off somewhere between the drowning and the pills.
Even with the show’s flaws, ending on that note will have even the biggest holiday grumps leaving the theater wearing a smile.
Jerry Zaks’s starry radio adaptation of Frank Capra’s classic has a moving finale, but its performances lack top-tier theatrical vitality.

Despite its sterling pedigree – the director is four-time Tony winner and Broadway legend Jerry Zaks, the scenic and costume design is by Santo Loquasto, and its lead producer is the tastemaking company Seaview
Unabashedly nostalgic without veering into schmaltz, It’s a Wonderful Life – A Live Radio Play , rings all the right bells.
The production, which ends with the cast singing Christmas carols, creates a gather-round-the-hearth sense of community and warmth.
It made me cry, and it put me in the Christmas spirit.
This adaptation could easily become a Broadway holiday staple; it's easy to mount and is family friendly.
Fans of the film will find plenty of angels in this radio-ready Bedford Falls, even if a production torn between heartfelt and hammy has to work a little harder to earn its wings.
Visually, it is a polished exercise in nostalgia: A 1940s radio broadcast recreated before a live audience, complete with all the period charm one could wish for.
The only cast member fully inhabiting his character, Andrew Rannells actually reminds one of Jimmy Stewart who originated the role.
The work should be called It’s a Sacrificial Life or It’s an Unexplored Life.
The idea of a radio show is interesting on paper, yet confusing in execution.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this holiday production—Rannells earns praise for his George Bailey, but many find the radio play format more decorative than dramatic, leaving it a pleasant yet lightweight seasonal diversion rather than a truly vital theatrical experience.

sn.c: The Mezzanine overhang is very obvious by row R, and views may be worse in rows R, S and T.
sn.sh: Obvious overhang and possibly worse views

sn.c: Three Boxes elevated above the Left Orchestra have unfixed chairs and are at quite sharp angles.
sn.sh: Unfixed chairs and quite sharp angles

sn.lo: Center Mezzanine, rows C to F
sn.c: Center Mezzanine rows C-F have enough rake to see over the top of heads, with elevated and wide sightlines at good value.
sn.sh: Elevated and wide sightlines at good value

sn.c: The cheapest seats are over to the sides of the Left and Right Mezzanine, where the view may be a little more restricted.
sn.sh: View may be a little more restricted

sn.lo: Center Mezzanine, rows A to D
sn.c: Center Mezzanine rows A to D give an elevated view for less than the premium Orchestra seats.
sn.sh: Rows A to D: elevated view for less

sn.c: The middle of Mezzanine rows can be very cramped, so pick an aisle seat if you want more legroom.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's least comfortable theaters, with notoriously tight legroom and narrow seats. The lack of rake means tall patrons in front block your view. Restrooms are in the basement, creating long intermission lines. For legroom, target Row A or N in Orchestra.

acc.note: 6 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.

vr.q: I wouldn't splurge to see this, but it is a perfectly fine production with the right expectations.
